::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From Fleet Operations to the Capstone System Synthesis"}
Over the preceding six parts of this curriculum, we have methodically constructed the engineering foundations of agentic machine learning systems. In Part I, we analyzed the computational engine, formalizing autoregressive decoding, KV cache memory dynamics, and test-time search. In Part II, we designed the memory hierarchy, establishing the operational boundaries between volatile working context, persistent retrieval indexes, and authoritative ground truth. In Part III, we addressed execution sandboxing, enforcing least privilege and Zero Ambient Authority ($A=0$) across mediated tool interfaces. In Part IV, we structured the runtime supervisor, implementing deterministic state machines, write-ahead logging, and compensating saga transactions. In Part V, we optimized agent policies through reinforcement learning and trajectory fine-tuning. And in Part VI, we scaled these architectures into distributed fleets, instrumenting distributed tracing, empirical evaluation benchmarks, and physical serving economics.

We now enter Part VII (*System Synthesis*). In the concluding capstone, Chapter 18 (*Architectural Synthesis*), we unite these distinct modules into a unified reference architecture. We synthesize the system invariants, verify interface contracts across the entire hierarchy, and evaluate real-world production case studies, demonstrating how the complete systems discipline enables the construction of robust, fault-tolerant, and economically viable autonomous agent systems.
:::
cumulative_ledger: Section 17.1 (Task Cost Accounting): True agent cost accounting encompasses model prefill/decode, tool API fees, sandbox compute time, assessment overhead, failed attempts, and human review costs—not merely model provider token rates.

Section 17.2 (Critical Path Latency): Trajectory latency is governed by the critical path of sequential dependencies; applying Amdahl's Law reveals when accelerating model generation yields diminishing returns compared to tool waits or environment resets.

Section 17.3 (Tiered Model Cascades): Optimal cost-performance engineering routes routine tasks and intermediate checks to lightweight, cheap models, reserving expensive frontier reasoning models for complex planning or escalation recovery.

Section 17.4 (Speculative Decoding Acceleration): Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation without altering the output probability distribution by drafting tokens with a small model and verifying them in parallel with the target model.

Section 17.5 (Fleet Capacity Provisioning): Capacity planning must distinguish short model invocations from long-lived trajectories and measure the distribution of each resource's occupancy; admission and scheduling policies follow the observed workload.

Section 17.6 (Monotonic Spending Governance): Production agent runtimes require monotonic token and financial budgets, hierarchical reservation ledgers across delegated child agents, and circuit breakers against runaway spending loops.

Section 17.7 (Architectural Selection Frameworks): The optimal agent architecture is a Pareto trade-off between task complexity, latency constraints, financial budget, and tolerable blast radius—ranging from deterministic scripts to bounded autonomous agents.

Section 17.8 (Serving Economics Synthesis): An end-to-end fleet economics architecture integrates task cost accounting, critical-path Amdahl analysis, tiered routing cascades, speculative decoding, and MLFQ capacity provisioning into a coherent economic control loop.
